items.title: The Fatal Combination of Ideology and Charisma
items.description: In January 1977, not two years before Reverend Jim Jones would orchestrate his followers’ deaths by the hundreds, a San Francisco church bestowed its Martin Luther King Jr. Humanitarian Award on him. Jones, the founder of the Peoples Temple of the Disciples of Christ, had managed to become a major player in the city’s politics. No one foresaw the horrific depths to which the combination of a charismatic leader, an all-encompassing belief system, and the human need for community and redemption would soon descend. On November 18, 1978, at Jones’s eponymous farm commune deep in the jungles of northwest Guyana, 908 members of the Peoples Temple, which had become a Pentecostalist-inspired socialist personality cult, either ingested cyanide-laced punch or were shot for refusing to do so. Most of the victims were poor Black Americans; more than 300 were children. Multiple generations of families died at Jonestown—grandmothers administered the deadly concoction to their screaming grandchildren before swallowing it themselves. (Based on a recording and other evidence from the incident, no one can say how many died willingly; men with guns oversaw the operation.) Just hours before, at a nearby airstrip, gunmen acting on Jones’s orders had murdered three journalists, a temple defector, and Representative Leo Ryan, a Bay Area Democrat who had traveled to Jonestown on behalf of temple members’ concerned relatives. Jones himself died from a gunshot wound to the head. Until 9/11, Jonestown had been the largest premeditated mass killing of American civilians in history. In his 1980 book, Journey to Nowhere: A New World Tragedy , the author Shiva Naipaul examines how ideologies related to the American counterculture helped bring about the massacre, and what he finds is deeply disturbing: Jonestown wasn’t just the work of only one man, Naipaul argues; it was also the product of a morally corrupted environment. [ James Kirchick: The DSA is a parasite ] The phrase drinking the Kool-Aid , a metaphor for unquestioningly holding a belief, was inspired by the fatal cocktail administered at Jonestown. But dark jokes about a nearly half-century-old massacre have a way of obscuring its continuing relevance. In recent years, totalizing ideologies such as communism, fascism, and Islamism have found dedicated audiences on social media, and the proliferation of demagogues manipulating people for malign ends is an ever-present worry. Jones himself was a mentally unsound megalomaniac. But the people who followed him to South America were not—poor and vulnerable, yes; crazy, no. During Naipaul’s too-brief career, he was overshadowed by his older brother, the Nobel laureate V. S. After the younger Naipaul died at 40, in 1985, his book about Jonestown languished in obscurity. Fortunately, Doubleday has reissued Journey to Nowhere as part of a new imprint called Outsider Editions, which aims to revive “extraordinary books” that “were overlooked or forgotten but still speak urgently to this moment.” The edition comes with a new introduction by the Pulitzer Prize–winning memoirist Hua Hsu, and it could not have arrived at a more opportune time. Naipaul, Hsu writes, was skeptical of worldviews whose adherents had “no interest in solutions to political problems” and “wanted to feel as though they were being saved.” Naipaul first came to understand how “the language of religion could be transformed into the language of politics” in his native Trinidad, where he once saw supporters of a future prime minister holding placards that declared him the Messiah. Fascinated by the decolonization of what was then called the Third World—the poor nations unaligned with either Cold War superpower—Naipaul traveled to Jonestown two weeks after the massacre in search of answers as to why the commune, which Jones had touted as a collectivist utopia, had gone so tragically wrong. In the second half of Journey to Nowhere , Naipaul takes us to what he sees as the real scene of the crime: Northern California, where Jones had built his flock and cultivated alliances with influential political figures. In the San Francisco of the early and mid-1970s, the Peoples Temple could blend in as just another piece of the city’s eccentric furniture. Jones began his ministry in 1950s Indianapolis, where he founded an interracial church. Seeking a more liberal environment, he moved to Northern California in 1965. Many Black parishioners who joined the Peoples Temple attested to the church’s racial inclusiveness. This perception was central to the positive reputation that Jones built up among San Francisco’s political elite—an image that persisted even after revelations of misconduct began to surface. In 1972, the San Francisco Examiner published a four-part investigation into abuse and financial impropriety within the church, and five years later, New West magazine reported on the physical and psychological terror that Jones inflicted on his followers . But Jones’s proven get-out-the-vote operation apparently eclipsed local officials’ misgivings. Jones’s ever more abusive and erratic behavior was ignored or rationalized by people who should have looked harder. State Assemblyman and future Mayor Willie Brown once praised Jones as an “American Gandhi,” a combination of Martin Luther King Jr., Angela Davis, Albert Einstein, and Mao Zedong (he meant this as a compliment). California Governor Jerry Brown attended a testimonial dinner held in Jones’s honor, and in 1976 the Democratic vice-presidential candidate, Walter Mondale, invited him onto his campaign plane. Nine months before the massacre, the city supervisor Harvey Milk, one of America’s first openly gay politicians, lauded Jones as a “man of the highest character” in a letter to President Jimmy Carter. These officials’ endorsements of Jones made him all the more dangerous to his followers, Naipaul argues. In his view, evildoers require passive and active enablers, whom he deems partly culpable for their deeds. “Those who ought to know better nourish our crazy dreams of resurrection and redemption; those safely beyond the borders of our madness underwrite our lunacies,” he writes; it’s the closest thing his book has to a thesis. California, in Naipaul’s words, was a “state of mind.” So too was the ideology that Jones embraced. The term Third Worldism was devised in the early years of the Cold War to define a system of beliefs that Hsu, in his introduction, characterizes as “an awakening of the global underclass.” In practice, it has usually amounted to a blend of socialism, authoritarianism, and rhetoric pitting the global South against the West. An antipathy to American racism, imperialism, and capitalism was the reason that Jones and his followers decamped in the summer of 1977 to Guyana—then well more than a decade into Prime Minister Forbes Burnham’s experiment with “cooperative socialism.” Oddly for a man of the cloth, Jones seemed to prioritize communism over religious belief. “Neither my colleagues nor I are any longer caught up in the opiate of religion,” he wrote , echoing Karl Marx’s denigration of divine faith. He referred to the Bible, its teachings so clearly at odds with his own mad project, as a “ paper idol ” and a “ dead letter .” On the day of the mass culling, as his desperate followers pleaded for their lives, Jones screamed at them to “stop this hysterics. This is not the way for people who are socialists or communists to die.” (Jones’s term for the events of that terrible day, “revolutionary suicide,” is the title of the Black Panther Party co-founder Huey Newton’s 1973 autobiography.) As temple members met their gruesome death, documents bequeathing some $7 million to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union were spirited out of Jonestown in a suitcase stuffed with cash. These statements and actions, some conservatives said at the time in a finger-wagging tone, demonstrated that mass suicide at the feet of a power-mad dictator was the predictable result of radical left-wing politics. Ruminating on the tragedy, the Catholic intellectual Michael Novak wrote that socialism “ begins in mysticism and ends in terror .” Yet Jones was driven by instincts more primal than politics. Yes, he had openly fantasized about relocating his church to the Soviet Union, producing what Naipaul describes as “a cruel fantasy of escape” that “led to the sad absurdity of eighty-year-old ‘senior citizens’ struggling to master an alien tongue and comprehend Lenin’s thoughts on Marx and Engels.” But Jones had also been on friendly terms with the San Francisco chapter of the John Birch Society, claimed to be saving taxpayer dollars by helping the poor, and donated money to the wives of slain police officers. He was a narcissist and an authoritarian before he was anything else. In Jonestown, the racial brotherhood that Jones had spoken about in San Francisco transmogrified into racial paternalism—or worse. An undercurrent of white supremacy was undeniable at Jonestown, where Black people labored in the fields for 11 hours a day on meager rations while Jones preached to them over a loudspeaker from the comfort of an air-conditioned house with a well-stocked larder. “Jones stripped bare his following and left them naked and defenseless,” Naipaul writes. “He did not liberate: he assaulted and traumatized those who believed in him. One can sense at a certain level his raging hatred for the Blacks whose God he claimed to be; a hatred so deep-seated, so tormenting that, in its fury, it turned itself inside out and called itself Love.” In spite of his conduct, Jones was skilled at speaking in a way that appealed to progressives and reinforced his left-wing bona fides. He cast the church’s critics as reactionaries hell-bent on destroying his radical ministry. To counter the media’s “vicious lies,” Jones enlisted Mark Lane, a dean of the President John F. Kennedy–assassination–conspiracy–theory industry, and Charles Garry, an attorney for the Black Panthers. After touring Jonestown in September 1978, Lane alleged that the settlement was being “cruelly assaulted by the intelligence organizations,” and Garry was convinced that, as Naipaul put it, “animals were better treated in Jonestown than human beings were in the United States.” Sycophants such as these, Naipaul writes, turned Jones into “a modern-day Moses,” such that when the preacher “did finally pull the trigger, he was able to pull it not only on himself but on nearly a thousand others.” To this day, conspiracy theories alleging that Jonestown was a CIA mind-control experiment gone awry find favor across the internet. [ Read: How much worse is this going to get? ] To some extent, Jones’s constant inveighing against fascism and genocide indicate his paranoia. But Naipaul reminds us about how ubiquitous premonitions of catastrophe and doom were in the 1970s. The optimism and idealism of the 1960s had curdled into what Tom Wolfe dubbed the “‘Me’ Decade .” Watergate, Vietnam, and stagflation sapped American confidence to a degree not seen since the Great Depression. During an 18-month period stretching from 1971 to 1972, the FBI recorded some 2,500 domestic-terror bombings . Fears about environmental devastation, overpopulation, energy depletion, and a nuclear holocaust were omnipresent, manifested in books such as The Population Bomb , the back-to-the-land movement, and the entire Hollywood disaster-movie genre. Owing more to Jones’s personality than to his politics, something like the horror in Guyana was inevitable, in Naipaul’s telling. But responsibility for it radiated widely, as “the ideological irresponsibilities of a promiscuous decade were coming home to roost in Jonestown.” Journey to Nowhere deserves to be read alongside Joan Didion’s Slouching Towards Bethlehem as a pair of bookends to the American counterculture. The ideology of Third Worldism and the New Agey, anything-goes-style progressivism of the West Coast that Naipaul so keenly lacerates were necessary precursors to the mass death in Guyana. But the most important factor distinguishing Jonestown from the other left-wing movements of its time was a singularly evil leader. Today, Americans routinely describe their political opponents—whether in the MAGA movement or the Democratic Socialists of America—as members of a cult . But whatever you think of Donald Trump or New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, neither of them is Jim Jones. Nearly half a century onward, Jonestown strikes many people as a bizarre aberration. Knowing everything that we now know about the Peoples Temple, we struggle to understand how anyone could have been taken in by Jones. That so many otherwise intelligent people missed the warning signs is a testament to the power of his message and the force of his charisma. The Washington Post correspondent Charles Krause didn’t realize the truth until he was dodging bullets at the nearby airstrip. “It seemed to me that the Peoples Temple had a legitimate purpose, a noble purpose, and was more or less succeeding,” he later wrote . The tragedy is not just that Jones deceived people. It’s also how willing they were to be deceived. Naipaul’s scathing critique of radical left-wing politics may yet limit the audience for his ideas. One recent review of Journey to Nowhere assails Naipaul for the “racism” of his analysis of Third Worldism and denigrates the book as “one long sneer” at “vegetarians, environmentalism, hippies, feminists,” and other progressive interests. Some of Naipaul’s language comes across as dated, and the scorn he feels for certain postcolonial political actors and their Western sympathizers is palpable. But his unsettling conclusions still warrant attention. At a time when more and more people look to politics for salvation , we should heed Naipaul’s warnings about how we see what we want to see and ignore what we don’t.

items.title: Longing for a Time Before Smartphones
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Gen Z has romanticized the technology of the ’90s—or the era’s lack of it. Young people long for a time when they were looking at one another instead of at their phones. But could that nostalgia for a smartphone-free society actually help guide the future? That’s one of the driving questions in the latest season of How to Touch Grass , co-hosted by Julie Beck and Natalie Brennan. This week on Radio Atlantic , we’re sharing the first episode, with an introduction by Hanna Rosin. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . Do I remember a time before I had a smartphone? Of course I do. [ Music ] Long dinners with friends, nothing buzzing or pinging. Standing in line with nothing to do but think, and stare. Reading an entire book in two days. And then back to when I was a teenager: telling my friends that I liked or maybe didn’t like their new perm, like, in person. I guess that’s what they call nostalgia? But nostalgia is working a little differently for Gen Z. I actually lived through the things I miss. But a lot of them long for a time when they weren’t even alive—an era of iPods and CD players and calling your friends on a landline. [ Music ] I find it strange that people in their 20s are now fixated on shows I watched when I was in my 20s, like Friends . It seems like longing that goes nowhere? But maybe nostalgia for the past, even an unfamiliar past, can help shape the future. Today we have something special: the first episode from How to Touch Grass . It’s the latest season of The Atlantic ’s How To series. It’s all about how we might renegotiate our relationships with technology and untangle ourselves from guilt and habit and mindless patterns. Step one: Go touch grass, probably. I’ll let co-hosts Julie Beck and Natalie Brennan take it from here. [ Music ] Julie Beck: If you had one word—it can be a noun, it can be an adjective, it can be any part of speech that you want—to describe your overall relationship to technology at this moment in time. Voice memo: Antagonistic? Voice memo: Complicated. Voice memo: Fraught. Voice memo: Connection. Voice memo: I think of it as an addiction. Similar to how I relate to, like, sugar or anything else that I sort of compulsively overindulge in. Beck: What’s your word? Voice memo: Indentured. Voice memo: I was gonna say reluctant, but maybe that’s not right. Voice memo: Very frequent user. Beck: Okay, that’s a lot of words, but we’ll take it. Beck: I’m Julie Beck, a staff writer at The Atlanti c. Natalie Brennan: And I’m Natalie Brennan, a producer at The Atlantic . Beck: This is How to Touch Grass . Amy Poehler : Have you heard the young people say “touch grass”? Tiktok user : I switched to a dumb phone. This is the Nokia 2780. Amy Poehler : It’s like a term, basically, which is like, Get off your phones . Subway Takes : Smartphones are evil, they’re ruining society, and we need to just stop. 100% disagree. Amy Poehler : Get off the internet, and go outside and touch grass. Tiktok user 2 : I nominate everyone for the Touch Grass Challenge. Go outside and touch some grass like I’m doing right now. Go, go, go! [ Birds chirping ] Beck: In this season, we’ll be exploring the often-fraught, always-changing relationship people have with technology. And the ways that, in this moment, the terms of the relationship are being renegotiated. Brennan: Julie, the way that I would like to renegotiate my relationship to technology is that I would like to throw my phone in the East River. Beck: Natalie, you could throw your phone in the East River. Why don’t you? Brennan: It’s not really just about my phone. I wanna throw your phone in there too, Julie. But I can’t take everyone’s phone. Beck: Mmm. Brennan: So I think what I mean to say is that I yearn for a pre-phone era. Beck: I think we’re not the only ones who have this fantasy. It’s all over TikTok. TikTok user : What’s the biggest trend of 2026 gonna be? Analog. This past year, we’ve seen the rise of nostalgia; the switch from iPhone cameras to digital cameras … TikTok user 2 : Here’s how to actually be more analog in 2026. First, I wanna … TikTok user 3 : The analog era is here. And while audiences say they want to go offline, with Gen Z and millennials openly expressing their desires to break from an online world and find deeper … TikTok user 4 : I stopped using an iPhone three weeks ago and the effects have genuinely been profound. ​ Beck: In the past few years, there’s been no shortage of people advocating for reducing screen time. But another force that has been inspiring people to rethink how they use their devices lately is: nostalgia. [ Music ] Clay Routledge: We can often feel overwhelmed in the moment and in the challenges we face today. It’s hard to see past them. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment. Beck: Clay Routledge and his colleagues have been studying what’s behind this widespread yearning for a time before smartphones and before social media. Clay is a psychologist who specializes in nostalgia, and he’s also the author of Past Forward: How Nostalgia Can Help You Live a More Meaningful Life . Beck: Clay, hello, welcome! Routledge : Hi, Julie. Beck: I see you’ve got an Atari poster behind you. There’s some kind of video game that is too small for me to see what it is. What is it? Routledge: On the shelf, I’ve got an old Nintendo, the original NES. Then I’ve got the Robotron arcade game, which is an arcade from the ’80s, and the Atari poster. So yeah, lots of video-game nostalgia from different brands and decades. Beck: Oh, man. Perfect. Okay. It’s a nostalgia museum at your house. Routledge: It is indeed. Beck: Clay, just to get started, what is the point of being nostalgic about anything? Routledge: So nostalgia is, in psychological terms, what we call a self-regulatory resource. It helps us navigate life in important ways. We don’t know the future; it’s uncertain. And so it can also be a great source of anxiety. Nostalgia can help us step outside of that moment and say, You know, there’s a bigger picture. Right now, maybe I’m experiencing stress or loneliness, or I just went through some difficult challenge, but my life is full of other types of experiences, and if I had these more fulfilling experiences in the past, then I should be able to have them in the future. Beck: Yeah, I asked you about the past, and you immediately started talking about the future. Do people tend to misunderstand nostalgia by assuming, as I did, that it’s about the past? Routledge: So nostalgia, the dictionary definition is something like: a sentimental longing for the past . When you present it like that, then it makes sense that people would assume, well, nostalgia might even be people getting stuck in the past. Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: Or looking to the past too warmly and not, you know, dealing with their present realities head-on. Turns out that when people engage in this kind of nostalgic reflection, in a lot of ways they’re talking about their issues today, and they’re thinking about tomorrow. So nostalgia actually has this very forward-looking, unexpected, hopeful quality. We often are looking for specific things that can help us with particular challenges and anxieties we’re facing, so— Beck: Mmm. Routledge: —and I’m articulating this as if this is happening at some deliberate or conscious level, ’cause I’m talking about more of the scientific study of nostalgia and what we’ve learned from that kind of empirical work. But in reality, of course, this is just happening almost unconsciously. People are often using nostalgia without even realizing it. Beck: That makes sense to me when it comes to, you know, my own life and my own past experiences, right? But Clay, what about nostalgia for a time from before you were even alive? There was a stat from a survey you worked on that really struck me, which was you found that 60 percent of Gen Z wished that they could return to a time before everyone was, quote, “plugged in.” And the other generations said that too, but they actually lived through that time, whereas Gen Z has no actual memories of a time before the internet existed. So was that surprising to you? Routledge: It was. When we first found that, I was pretty surprised because most of the work, the research on nostalgia, including the research I’ve done, is focused on autobiographical— Beck: Mm. Routledge: —memory, but to your point, what we started to discover with that survey is: People actually have a longing for the past that predates them. Now, of course, if you’ve studied art and culture more abstractly, we’ve long known that people have favorite eras that they’re interested in, whether it’s the architecture or the music or the fashion. So we’ve known there’s this aesthetic nostalgia that’s historical— Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: —but what we were surprised to find is that young adults have so much to look forward to in the future, and we typically think of youth as very future-oriented, but the majority of them were saying that they longed for a time really before modern technology, but really before they were alive. And then since that survey, we’ve just done more and more surveys finding that around two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they’re nostalgic for a time before they were alive. Beck: Right. So this seems like a little bit more than just a like, We’re bringing low-rise jeans back , right?— Routledge: ( Laughs. ) Yeah. Beck: —if they’re saying they would like to live in the past. I mean, how common is it for generations to yearn that way for a past they never actually knew, or is something about this unique? Routledge: Yeah. There’s not a lot of research or really any research in previous generations when they were the same age as Gen Z. But we do know from our own work, in general, people tend to become nostalgic when they’re going through major life transitions or disruptions, or when the world feels particularly chaotic or uncertain. Beck: Mmm. Routledge: Regardless of whether you’re, you know, 20 or 60, sometimes there are sources of cultural inspiration that people wanna draw from in a more shared bank of memories that aren’t just your own, but are the memories we share as a culture. And here’s the key thing, I think, and this is the case with Gen Z too. It really isn’t the case that people want to live in the past. Beck: Okay. Routledge: If you start asking people Would they give up all of the modern advances? they say no. What they’re saying is they have a sentiment for some aspect of the past that they think that we’re missing today. I think there is something about Gen Z in this, you know, as digital natives who grew up in this era where this major transition from the analog world to the digital world, that seems to be sparking a particularly potent type— Beck: Yeah. Routledge: —of historical nostalgia. And then the irony is technology really is helping facilitate this. Because how are Gen Z adults learning about retro trends? They’re on TikTok, right? Beck: Yeah. Routledge: And so it’s funny how the technology that, on the one hand, is the source of frustration and anxiety is also the vehicle through which they’re being introduced to the analog world. Beck: Okay, so, I was wondering because, you know, when you say you wanna return to another era, an earlier era, maybe they’re not thinking about the things they would be dissatisfied with in the earlier era, right? Like— Routledge: Right. Beck: —lack of social progress that we have since made. It seems like you’re saying it tends to be about something particular that they are yearning for rather than, like, a holistic desire to go back to all the things. Routledge: Yeah, absolutely. You know, one of the things I think people don’t appreciate about nostalgia, ’cause it’s often portrayed as just repeating something. Beck: Mm. Routledge: And it really isn’t. It’s more of, like, a revising. There’s a creative process. Humans are really a progress-oriented species. We’re never content; we’re never satisfied. We’re always tinkering. We always think things can be a little bit better, and it’s frustrating, right? Because it often means we’re not ever just really happy. But that’s also the thing that drives us to positive change, and nostalgia’s very much an ingredient of that. [ Music ] Beck: So Natalie, I can remember really distinctly the last time that I was ever truly lost. Brennan: Mm-hmm. Beck: It was like two months before I would get my first smartphone. The year was 2013. Brennan: So you were—how old were you then? Beck: I was 23. Brennan: Okay. Beck: I was in St. Petersburg, Russia, and what I would do to get around in the days before I had Google Maps available on my phone all the time is I would look up directions on the computer before I left, and I would write them down, sometimes on my hand. Brennan: Totally. Beck: I had done this: I’d gotten my directions together, I had gone sightseeing, and I was heading back to my hotel. But I was so jet-lagged that I fell asleep on the bus, and when I woke up, I had no idea if I’d already missed my stop or not. Brennan: Oh no. Do you speak Russian? Beck: I definitely don’t. Um, but I went up to the bus driver anyways, to try to ask him if we had already passed the stop. A lot of people spoke English, you know, but he got really angry and was like, “You can’t talk to me while I’m driving.” So he wouldn’t talk to me, and I’m freaking out. And this young woman behind me, she can see how upset I am, and she speaks English. So she comes up and tells me, like, yes, we already passed the stop for my hotel. Lovely woman. She gets off the bus with me at the next stop— Brennan: No! Beck: —and she drew me a map on a piece of paper that she had, and she was like, “There’s this one really long road. You just have to walk on that road the whole way back.” And the hotel was on that road, so you would see it, you know, looming in the distance. And I remember she said, “It's really far. You’re gonna think that you’re never gonna get there, but I promise if you just keep walking on this one road, you will get back to the hotel.” Brennan: Oh my God. I’d be crying. Were you crying? Beck: Oh, for sure. Brennan: Yeah. ( Laughs. ) Beck: So anyway, I set off down the road for a really long time. It felt like miles, multiple miles. Brennan: You’re alone. Beck: I’m alone. I was traveling alone. When, out of nowhere, this man comes running towards me. Brennan: Nope. Beck: Well, it turns out he’s from a cruise ship that is docked nearby, and he is trying to find McDonald’s. Brennan: No. Beck: I tell him what happened. And he says, “Oh, well that’s the same direction as my cruise ship that I need to get back to. Like, I’ll just walk with you until you get back.” Eventually, my hotel appears on the horizon, finally. And there’s really no other word for it; he, like, scampers off into the night, and as he runs away, he shouts, “Goodbye, Julie. I love you.” Brennan: No! Beck: So anyway, I made it home safely. And that was the last time I was ever lost in my life. Brennan: Wow. I’m feeling both jealousy and awe, in that I will—I’ve never had that experience. I mean, I’ve been on public transportation, of course, while my phone has died. Beck: Yeah. Brennan: But I have never been an adult without a smartphone. Beck: I am kind of nostalgic for that memory, because it was one of those moments that really restores your faith in humanity. You know? Brennan: Yeah. Beck: Like, I was screwed, and people appeared, and they helped me when I really needed it. And that made me feel, like, swaddled tightly in the fabric of human community. And none of that would’ve happened if I had a smartphone, if I had Google Maps. Brennan: Yeah. I’ve only really ever had that experience manufactured for me. Beck: Really? Brennan: Yes. I went on this program in college. It was called the New England Literature Program. Beck: Okay. Brennan: And it’s basically living in cabins on a lake in New Hampshire for six weeks. And when you arrive, they take your phone for the remainder of the program. There’s no personal technology, no phones, no computers. Beck: Hmm. Brennan: You read Emerson, Thoreau. Beck: Of course you do. Who else would you read? Brennan: You visit Walden Pond. ( Laughs. ) And on the second day of the program is Get Lost Day. Beck: Okay. Brennan: In the morning, we learned how to use a compass, and then, promptly, were blindfolded, which now sounds like a cult, but it wasn’t— Beck: ( Laughs. ) Brennan: —to different locations, in groups, and then shown on a map where we were and where camp was, and told to get back by dinner. Beck: Wait, wait, wait. Where—like, describe to me the vibe of, like, where— Brennan: We were dropped off? Field. Beck: Field. End of sentence? Brennan: Yep. Beck: Field. Okay, okay, okay. Brennan: In the beginning, you’re quite confident that you’re on track, and I think a few hours in, it became quite clear to us that we weren’t making it back to camp, and that we would just find a ride later in the day. We would ask somebody to take us back to camp, and just kind of spent the day enjoying and exploring. Beck: Oh, wow. So you just pivoted. You were like, This is never happening. We’re not gonna find our way back. Brennan: No. Beck: Let's just be in this field. Brennan: We’re gonna—we are going to touch grass and vibe. Beck: Okay. Brennan: I’m sure we were walking for hours, but I think the bigger point, instead, was to, like, get to know each other. You’re placed into vulnerability. You’re going to share this experience. But I do think extremely fondly about the program. Those whole six weeks really just sparkle with nostalgia for me, and I really struggle to differentiate between how much of that experience was the “no tech” of it all— Beck: Hmm Brennan: —and how much of it was just the experience at large. [ Music ] Beck: Clay, what do you think the thing is that people who are nostalgic for the ’90s or the 2000s are wanting to bring forward and revise, as you say? Routledge: If I could sum it up using two words. Beck: That’d be great. Routledge: I would say control and community . Beck: Mm. Routledge: And the reason I’m picking those two words is because we’ve done, in addition to the surveys, we’ve done a number of qualitative projects that, you know, look at the types of nostalgic-related posts that Gen Z adults make on different social media and websites that they frequent. And what you often find is this sense that they love technology, but they wanna be in control of it, not feel controlled by it. Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: So it’s that more sense of intentional use, and this is why I think you see these interesting trends like Gen Z buying old iPods and, you know, they wanna have their new iPhone. Everybody wants to have the Uber app and all the different things that make our lives a little more convenient, but sometimes there’s a sense of like, Maybe there’s a more low-tech option that allows me just to listen to music . Beck: Yeah. Routledge: And the community. I think Gen Z’s figuring out that there’s something missing in computer-mediated social relationships. And on the one hand, the social media’s really useful ’cause it helps you organize events, meet people you would’ve never met. But at the same time, they look at this time period right before smartphones really became dominant, and they said, Oh, there’s a sense of freedom. There’s a sense of organic social life , and— Beck: You’re not looking at your phone the whole time. Routledge: —mm hmm. And they want to build that in. A lot of times, nostalgia’s framed in a very zero-sum sort of framework, where it’s like: You’re either for the past or you’re for the future. And I think what Gen Z’s showing us is they want both. And there’s something to say intergenerationally about this, which is maybe young people are learning about ’90s fashions on TikTok, but then what we often find is that sparks a conversation with older generations, whether it’s a parent or a coworker you know, or somebody in their run club, that they’re like, Oh, was life really like this? Did you really do this? And it creates a dialogue between generations, which I think, in this era of where everyone has their own screens and their own tailored content, is something that people feel like they’re really missing. Beck: Yeah. I remember my dad always used to talk about that—that sort of, like, shared experience of music, ’cause you had to, like, put on a record, and so everybody’s listening to the Rolling Stones whether they like it or not. And now, obviously, we just have our sort of, like, isolated pods, and you don’t know that I’m listening to that same Taylor Swift song like 10 times in a row, and you’ll never know. Routledge: ( Laughs. ) Now I know. Beck: Okay. Yeah, I did—yeah, now everybody knows. [ Music ] Beck: We’re gonna take a quick break. When we come back: Why is this analog nostalgia bubbling up now? Do you think it has anything to do with AI coming on the scene? [ Break ] Beck: Clay, why do you think nostalgia for analog technology is so popular right now ? Does the buzz about AI have anything to do with it? Routledge: I think AI is part of it, because if machines can do all this cognitive work, and maybe even creative work, that we thought was the distinct domain of humanity, now you’re seeing more of this holistic thinking of like, what is the essence of being a person? Beck: Mm-hmm. Routledge: And this nostalgia, I think, is really helping people get that sense of embodiment, of like, this isn’t just cognition. There’s something about emotion, spirituality, living in the world, having these tactile sensory experiences, in-person, real contact with other real human beings. Beck: Just with like, all the parts of life that are more than just being a brain in a jar, basically? Routledge: Yeah, that’s a great way of putting it. And if you look at a lot of the consumer nostalgic trends, many of them driven by Gen Z, they’re very much that, right? They’re the rise of independent bookstores , the growth of music festivals , book clubs , game nights, old tech, technology that’s not online that you have to—I was talking to somebody the other day about retro video games, and they were saying, “Well, one thing that’s really cool is you have to sit next to each other to play, like two players.” Beck: Yeah. Routledge: You’re not playing online. And so I think there’s this idea that even if it’s technology, even if it’s like video games or music, you mentioned vinyl records, which, you know, one of the big drivers of vinyl-record sales is Gen Z. They’re these low-tech, retro-tech trends that really seem to be about being out in the world, handling things, engaging with people. That’s a big driver of this. [ Music ] Beck: Natalie, let’s play a little game where I name a thing that people might be nostalgic for, and then try to psychoanalyze what it means about what they actually want from their relationship to technology. Brennan: Okay. Beck: Okay, my first one: I see a lot of memes about people missing the days when people had computer rooms in their home. Like, picture a big wooden entertainment center with a big monitor. The shelves are all covered in CD-ROMs, and then the meme says something like, We used to respect the computer. What does this mean? Brennan: This is really giving that control element that Clay was talking about— Beck: Mm. Brennan: —in that we still want to honor our computer. We love computer time, right? But I think we miss that separation in which your technology wasn’t on you at all times, right? My phone is kind of just a mini computer at this point. Beck: Yeah. Brennan: So I think we like having some separation of, like, now it’s time for me to go in the computer room, and when I’m done, it’s done. Does that resonate with you? Beck: Yeah. It’s a deliberate choice to go in the computer room and sit your butt in front of it and use it and then leave. Brennan: And then leave. Beck: I think you’re onto something. Okay, I am personally very nostalgic for Google Reader— Brennan: Mm. Beck: —which, for those who may not know, it was an aggregation service for websites’ RSS feeds, which doesn't sound fun, but it was. Brennan: ( Laughs .) Beck: Um, basically, in the late 2000s, I would use this to, like, follow all my favorite blogs and cooking websites and news sources, and it was all in one place. What do you think I’m actually longing for here? Brennan: Okay, well, I think for me what comes up here is feeling like the internet isn’t anymore curated towards what I wanna see. So for example, like I’ll open my Instagram app and I no longer see posts by my friends and family who I follow, but instead I see a lot of pushed posts. The algorithm just sends me what it thinks I wanna see. And so maybe you’re yearning for that time where the internet was curated to your niche hobbies and what you are actually interested in. Beck: As opposed to just a bunch of slop. Brennan: Okay, I wanna ask you one. I am also one of the analog Gen Zers who love to shoot film and collect old cameras. Thoughts? Beck: Um, I don’t know about you, but sometimes I pick up my phone to take a picture of probably my cats, and before I know it, I’m, like, sucked into a million other things on my phone. Brennan: Mm-hmm. Beck: So I think, maybe, there’s also something about, like, when you wanna take a picture, you just wanna take a picture, and taking that function out of the everything device and letting it just be its own thing, maybe. Brennan: It’s that. Beck: Crushed it. [ Music ] Beck: Clay, I was fascinated to learn that back in the 17th to 19th century, nostalgia was considered a disease , and doctors tried to cure it with leeches. I read that there was this one American doctor who kind of thought the way to cure it was just bullying people, like shaming them with public ridicule. And, obviously, we no longer think nostalgia is literally a disease, but I think a thread of that negative attitude remains. I feel like I sometimes hear other people talk about nostalgia as though you’re trying to hide from reality, and maybe, you know, you should be a little embarrassed. Do you see that reaction from people when it comes to this current cultural yearning for a pre-digital era that, okay, it’s not a disease , but maybe it’s still not good for you? Routledge: Yeah, definitely. People seem to have this view of nostalgia as anti-progress or holding people back from progress, and I spend a fair amount of time trying to disabuse them of that view and show them decades of empirical research. It really isn’t holding people back. We all have to adjust to change, and nostalgia helps people navigate that in the best way that they can. Even people who don’t think nostalgia’s a barrier to progress, oftentimes you see it characterized as a waste of time. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: Like, it’s a trivial thing, and it’s a distraction at best. Actually, nostalgia increases goal motivation . It increases a sense of meaning in life. It increases optimism. It makes people more creative . It increases empathy . Most nostalgic memories are social memories, so nostalgia actually pushes us towards each other. Beck: When you’re saying that some people are seeing nostalgia as an impediment to progress, do you think some of that has to do with the sort of Make America Great Again brand of nostalgia where, like you’re saying, people are looking to the past to potentially bring things into the future, but sometimes what they want to bring into the future is, for instance, stricter and more stereotypical gender roles? Routledge: So declinism is the view that things are getting worse and the past was better, whereas nostalgia really is just more of this warm feeling for the past, and I think the two are often conflated. We also find, overwhelmingly, that most of the time, nostalgia in general makes us see the humanity in other people. Or another way of saying it is: Nostalgia might be helping people wrestle with declinism— Beck: I see. Routledge: —and hopefully in a more productive and constructive way. A lot of Gen Z might feel like, oh, things are going in the wrong direction and their future’s gonna be worse than the future of previous generations. And there's certainly, you know, a lot of data that support that. Nostalgia’s helping them feel agentic and say, Well, you know what? We can change that. We can do something else . Beck: It just feels surprising when you see an era that was not a great time for a lot of people recast as something to be nostalgic for. Routledge: There are people that have nostalgia for COVID, which, again, not that long ago. Beck: Not that fun, famously. Routledge: Not that fun. But you know what? What’s interesting is, that wasn’t that surprising to me. When I first started doing this research, I was a professor at the University of Southampton in England. And Southampton’s a city that was heavily bombed during World War II, as a port city, and a good chunk of the city was destroyed. Not a good time. When we were doing this research, this was a little over 20 years ago, we were collecting nostalgic narratives from older British adults. Many of them were young children during that time, and they had this nostalgia. Beck: Yeah. Routledge: But what it was is they were saying, Well, this was a time that was defining, character defining. It wasn’t a pleasant time. It shaped our character, shaped our view of the world, shaped our ability to appreciate what’s important in life. Beck: So how does this sort of personal, individual nostalgia, right, then grow and end up becoming a cultural moment or an internet trend? Routledge: ’Cause a lot of times what people are really looking for with nostalgia is an opportunity to share memories. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: Oftentimes, nostalgia is portrayed as this very isolating, personal experience. After all, this is in your head. You’re experiencing this emotion. But people love opportunities where they can talk about nostalgic experiences, particularly ones where they might have their own idiosyncratic memory of it, but it was shared with other people. Beck: Mmm. Routledge: I think this is why people have a nostalgia for television where you had to wait and everyone had to watch the show at the same time, and then the next day we could all talk about it. Beck: Yeah. Routledge: You know, people are looking for ways to make contact over shared experiences where their personal nostalgia is woven into a broader cultural nostalgia that connects us. Beck: And we’ve talked about control a good amount, and, you know, obviously we can’t actually travel back in time to an era when nobody had smartphones. Sam Altman is gonna keep making new iterations of ChatGPT, and I have no control to stop him. But do the things that we’re nostalgic for hold any lessons for how we can exert the control that we do have over the role tech plays in our lives? Routledge: When the broader world outside of yourself, when you scale out, when it feels like you don’t have any control over that, that can be anxiety provoking; if you just focus your attention on your corner of the world, we actually do have a lot more control. Agency often happens at a local and at a personal level. You can help your neighbors. You can help your family. You can help your friends. You can be involved with those things. And even media engagement’s a way to remind ourselves of that. It’s like, Yeah, I don’t have control over the next internet iteration of a particular technology, but I can go to that retro store down the street and buy some Blu-ray discs and have a movie night at my house and have some people over. Beck: Yeah. Routledge: So I think people are really seeking that kind of experience. Beck: Are you seeing people actually acting on this pre-digital nostalgia? Routledge: There is an increased sales in physical media. The live-music market is growing. Mass attendance is up, like young people going to church. Beck: Right. Routledge: The number of independent bookstores and the number of chain bookstores, like Barnes & Nobles, is growing. There does seem to be something changing in our culture that’s a push back to the in-person and the analog. Beck: Clay, I’ve noticed at many times in this conversation that you’re very optimistic about Gen Z, which is not how I often hear people talking about that generation, especially when it comes to tech. So I’m curious to hear a little bit more about how you’re thinking about it and whether Gen Z is kind of leading this trend for other generations. Routledge: My thinking on Gen Z has really evolved, so I’m way more bullish on Gen Z— Beck: Hmm. Routledge: —than I used to be. So I’m a psychologist, and so when all of this research was coming out about these growing mental-health problems that young people were facing and how Gen Z reported higher rates of depression, anxiety, loneliness, pessimism for the future, like everyone else, I was like, This isn’t good. Young people are supposed to be the ones that are optimistic. They’re supposed to be the ones that look to the future with possibility, and that didn’t seem to be the case. But then I started really studying this historical nostalgia and started seeing, like, yeah, Gen Z has their challenges, and maybe mental health is one of them, but they’re not just sitting there doing nothing about it. They’re using their creativity and their problem-solving capacities that all humans have to do something about it, and I feel like this historical nostalgia that they’re engaging in is just one example of that. It’s not people my age that remember that time. It’s Gen Z that are saying, Hey, maybe we’re spending too much time online . And so, for instance, there’s surveys showing that Gen Z are the generation most likely to report disconnecting from their digital devices. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: So now I have a different view. It’s a, you know, it’s not a certain view, of course. It’s an optimistic view, though, that Gen Z might not only be doing better than we think they are in navigating their challenges and having the agency to do so, but they actually might lead us out of this mess. They might be the ones that remind the rest of us that there is an in-person, real-world life. So, you know, I often say that it’s common for people to feel sorry for Gen Z and worry that as digital natives, they were born too late to really appreciate the analog world. Beck: Hmm. Routledge: But in reality, it might be that they’re the generation that leads us back to it. [ Music ] Brennan: Mmmm …? Beck: It sounds like you’re not so sure, Natalie. Brennan: I said I wanted to throw my phone in the East River, and suddenly now I am tasked with healing everyone’s relationship to technology. Beck: Not just you. Just you and your entire generation are responsible for the rest of us? Uh … Brennan: I don’t know. I get so frustrated about this because I feel like I hear it all the time. It’s the same thing with climate change. Like, We’ll be the ones that need to fix all of it. I’m just like, This list is getting a little bit long. We’ve got a lot to fix now. Beck: Honestly, I think what talking to Clay made me realize is that so many of us are just looking for inspiration on how to move forward with technology in a way that doesn’t feel bad. Because we have to live in 2026. Brennan: Yeah. Beck: It’s never gonna be 1996 again. Brennan: Right. I think as a joint mission, then I can get behind that. Beck: When, like, Gen Z doesn’t have to be the leader, nobody’s the leader, nobody’s the follower, we’re just figuring it out together. Brennan: Yeah, or even bigger picture, when I feel like this is just on each one of us individually versus, you know, something that we’re all just, like, trying to renegotiate together. When it’s an individual mission, I think that’s maybe when I go escapist mode, when I go, like, fantasize about throwing the phone in the river, I wanna go back in time, back to those New England woods, to no phone. Beck: Back to your fields, back to your compass. Brennan: Yeah, back to my grass. [ Music ] Beck: That’s all for this episode of How to Touch Grass . This episode was hosted by me, Julie Beck, and co-hosted and produced by Natalie Brennan. Our editors are Claudine Ebeid and Jocelyn Frank. Fact-check by Gisela Salim-Peyer. Our engineer is Rob Smierciak. Rob also composed some of the music for this show. The executive producer of audio is Claudine Ebeid, and the managing editor of audio is Andrea Valdez. Beck: Next time on How To Touch Grass: Ashleigh Golden: A priest, a partner, a therapist, or a friend—these people have natural limits. They get tired. They push back. But the chatbot doesn't. Elias Aboujaoude: These programs are trained to be endlessly validating and endlessly agreeable. Beck: Turning to AI for help with anxiety could actually end up making you more anxious. That’s next time on How to Touch Grass .

items.title: Accident tragique entre deux bus de transport voyageurs : Mise au point du Ministre des transports à l’encontre des sociétés impliquées
items.description: Le Ministre des Transports et de l’Aviation Civile, Colonel-Major Abdouramane Amadou, a tenu, le lundi 10 août 2026, une rencontre de mise au point avec les responsables des sociétés de transport voyageurs STM et SONITRAV, impliquées dans le tragique accident survenu le vendredi 7 août 2026 dans la région de Maradi. Cet accident a malheureusement occasionné vingt-deux (22) décès, trente-sept (37) blessés, ainsi que d’importants dégâts matériels. Selon le communiqué « Face aux responsables des deux compagnies, le Ministre a durci le ton. Sans langue de bois, il a rappelé la gravité de la situation, dans des termes choisis pour poser clairement ce problème récurrent et en débattre sans détour ». « Il a jugé inacceptable que ce type de drame, dont la cause fondamentale demeure le comportement humain, continue d’endeuiller les populations nigériennes, alors même que l’État a engagé un vaste programme national de sensibilisation, à tous les niveaux, pour réduire significativement le nombre d’accidents de la route au Niger. » souligne le ministre dans le communiqué. « Il a appelé à des solutions appropriées, à mettre en œuvre dans les meilleurs délais, afin de mettre un terme aux comportements imprudents et irresponsables de certains conducteurs routiers, ainsi qu’à l’indulgence dont font parfois preuve leurs employeurs à cet égard », ajoute le communiqué, selon lequel « À travers une projection vidéo, le Ministre a entendu les deux parties sur leurs parts de responsabilité respectives dans cet accident, avant de leur donner des instructions fermes pour corriger les manquements constatés. » Le Ministre a clairement indiqué que des sanctions seront prises à l’encontre de la société dont la responsabilité dans cet accident sera établie, conformément à la réglementation en vigueur régissant le transport de voyageurs. Ces sanctions pourront aller, selon la gravité des manquements retenus, de l’avertissement à la suspension, voire au retrait de l’agrément d’exploitation, sans préjudice des poursuites judiciaires que pourraient engager les autorités compétentes. Cette rencontre s’est déroulée en présence des cadres centraux du Ministère des Transports et de l’Aviation Civile, des responsables de l’Agence Nigérienne de Sécurité Routière (ANISER) et de ceux de la Gendarmerie nationale. Par Agence nigerienne de presse L’article Accident tragique entre deux bus de transport voyageurs : Mise au point du Ministre des transports à l’encontre des sociétés impliquées est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Santé et enseignement supérieur : Oligui Nguema accélère la modernisation des infrastructures publiques
items.description: En poursuivant sa tournée de terrain dans le Grand Libreville, le président de la République, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, a progressé dans sa politique de modernisation des services publics. Entre la remise d’équipements médicaux de dernière génération au CHUL, l’inauguration du Laboratoire national de santé publique (LNSP) rénové et le suivi des travaux d’extension de l’Université des Sciences de la Santé, le chef de l’État réaffirme son ambition de renforcer durablement les secteurs de la santé et de la formation. Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, le directeur général du CHUL et le ministre de la Santé, lors de la remise des équipements, le 12 août 2026. © Communication présidentielle Le président de la République, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, a effectué le 12 août 2026 une nouvelle visite de terrain dans le Grand Libreville, marquée par plusieurs actions en faveur du renforcement du système sanitaire national. Au Centre hospitalier universitaire de Libreville (CHUL), le chef de l’État a remis un important lot d’équipements biomédicaux et de matériel roulant destiné à améliorer la qualité des soins et les capacités opérationnelles de l’établissement. Cette dotation comprend notamment des échographes, des aspirateurs de mucosités, des moniteurs multiparamétriques ainsi qu’une Imagerie par résonance magnétique (IRM). Deux ambulances figurent également parmi les équipements remis. Cette initiative intervient quelques semaines après une opération similaire réalisée au Centre Hospitalier Universitaire d’Owendo. À travers ces acquisitions, les autorités entendent renforcer les capacités de diagnostic et de prise en charge des patients tout en améliorant la réactivité des services hospitaliers. Lors de la cérémonie, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema a exhorté les responsables des structures bénéficiaires à faire preuve de rigueur dans l’utilisation et l’entretien du matériel mis à leur disposition. Il a insisté sur la nécessité de préserver ces équipements afin d’en garantir la durabilité et d’assurer aux populations un accès durable à des soins de qualité. Inauguration du Laboratoire national de santé publique rénové Quelques étapes de la tournée du chef de l’État. © Communication présidentielle Dans la continuité de cette visite, le président de la République a procédé à l’inauguration du Laboratoire national de santé publique entièrement réhabilité et agrandi. Les travaux réalisés ont permis de porter sa superficie de 750 à 1 250 mètres carrés et d’augmenter sa capacité d’accueil de 20 à 39 salles. Dotée d’équipements biomédicaux modernes, cette infrastructure est désormais mieux armée pour assurer les analyses et diagnostics liés notamment aux maladies à potentiel épidémique. « Cette modernisation permettra de réduire significativement les délais de diagnostic et de renforcer les capacités nationales de surveillance sanitaire », ont souligné les responsables du laboratoire. Le chef de l’État s’est félicité de cette avancée qui s’inscrit dans la volonté gouvernementale de faire du système de santé gabonais un véritable pôle d’excellence sous-régional. Les responsables des structures concernées ont, pour leur part, exprimé leur reconnaissance au président de la République et réaffirmé leur engagement à assurer une gestion optimale des équipements reçus au bénéfice des populations. En marge de ces activités, le président de la République s’est rendu à Owendo pour évaluer l’état d’avancement des travaux d’extension de l’Université des Sciences de la Santé (USS). Lancé en 2024, le projet affiche un taux d’exécution de 70 % et couvre une superficie de 6 000 mètres carrés. Le futur complexe comprendra notamment un amphithéâtre de 600 places, une salle de conférence, des espaces administratifs ainsi que des salles de cours pouvant accueillir jusqu’à 1 600 étudiants. À travers cet investissement, les autorités ambitionnent d’améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage et de travail des étudiants et enseignants, confirmant ainsi la place centrale accordée au développement du capital humain dans la stratégie de transformation du pays. L’article Santé et enseignement supérieur : Oligui Nguema accélère la modernisation des infrastructures publiques est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Bloctel piraté : 3 millions de numéros fuités juste avant sa fermeture
items.description: L'incident de securite a ete officialise par la Direction generale de la concurrence, de la consommation et de la repression des fraudes (DGCCRF). Bloctel, censé nous protéger du démarchage, a laissé fuiter les numéros de ses inscrits, et la DGCCRF confirme le piratage juste avant la fermeture du service. 👉 https://t.co/IHQJcfrAVc pic.twitter.com/L9t3EShbIu — Frandroid (@Frandroid) August 13, 2026 Un tiers non autorise a usurpe un compte professionnel pour telecharger des fichiers echanges avec le service Bloctel, contenant des numeros transmis par des professionnels et ceux restitues apres verification. Une fuite est survenue a la veille de la fin de Bloctel Les personnes concernees ont recu un courriel les informant que leur numero etait touche. « Aucune donnee personnelle associee a ces numeros n'a ete obtenue », assure la Repression des fraudes, qui precise que la base de donnees elle-meme n'a pas ete compromise. La CNIL a ete notifiee. Cette confirmation intervient dans un contexte particulier : Bloctel a definitivement ferme le 11 août 2026, dans un contexte de fermeture des centres d'appel affectant tout particulierement le Maroc et la Tunisie . La loi du 30 juin 2025 impose desormais un consentement explicite, prealable et tracable avant tout appel commercial. Le systeme d'opt-out, juge inefficace, a cede la place a un regime d'opt-in. Les professionnels doivent pouvoir prouver l'accord du consommateur, valable un an maximum et revocable a tout moment. Sur X, les critiques fusent. Virginie Debuisson, specialiste en affaires publiques et influence, interroge ironiquement : « On a des news de France Passoire. Piratage non confirme par la DGCCRF pour l'heure. Je me demande quelles donnees personnelles et sensibles ne sont pas en libre service sur le darkweb. » On a des news de France Passoire Piratage non confirmé par la DGIFP pour l’heure. Je me demande quelles données personnelles et sensibles 🇫🇷 ne sont pas en libre service sur le darkweb. #cybersecurité https://t.co/gICapBng4n — Virginie Debuisson (@VirgoWhallala) August 12, 2026 La DGCCRF appelle a la vigilance face aux sollicitations inhabituelles. Meme avec le nouveau cadre, les appels frauduleux ou provenant de l'etranger restent possibles. Les consommateurs peuvent signaler les abus sur SignalConso. items.title: Festival Cinémas d’Afrique de Lausanne : La Djeliya du Mandé sur les écrans
items.description: © Daou La 20 ème édition du Festival Cinémas d’Afrique de Lausanne se tient du 13 au 16 août 2026 au Casino de Montbenon. Parmi les œuvres programmées, « Djeliya, mémoire du Mandé » met en lumière la transmission de la mémoire dans les sociétés mandingues. La culture mandingue s’invite sur les écrans de Lausanne. Pour cette édition anniversaire, le festival propose plus de 60 œuvres venues de 29 pays, entre fictions, documentaires et films d’animation. La programmation accorde une place importante aux récits de transmission, aux parcours d’émancipation et aux femmes qui transforment leur environnement. Dans cet ensemble d’œuvres, « Djeliya, mémoire du Mandé », du réalisateur burkinabè Boubacar Sangaré, occupe une place particulière. Coproduit notamment au Mali par DS Productions, le documentaire suit Sékou Timité, un jeune griot malien engagé dans un voyage à travers l’espace mandingue. Le film sera projeté les 13 et 15 août au Cinématographe, en présence du réalisateur. D’une durée de 112 minutes, le long métrage est présenté à Lausanne en malinké et en bambara, avec des sous-titres en français. Il accompagne son protagoniste dans une quête où l’apprentissage de la parole, des récits et des codes du métier dialogue avec la mémoire de Soundiata Keïta et l’héritage historique du Mandé. Transmission À travers ce parcours, Boubacar Sangaré plonge dans l’univers des Djeli, détenteurs d’une parole transmise de génération en génération. Leur fonction dépasse la musique. Ils conservent les récits familiaux, les généalogies, les histoires des communautés et une mémoire collective liée aux grandes figures du Mandé. Longtemps portée par l’oralité, la djeliya doit aujourd’hui composer avec les transformations sociales, les nouveaux usages culturels et les attentes de générations davantage connectées. Le documentaire interroge ainsi la manière dont cet héritage se perpétue, s’adapte et trouve sa place dans le monde contemporain. Le voyage de Sékou Timité permet aussi de montrer que la djeliya dépasse les frontières du Mali et demeure partagée par plusieurs sociétés en Afrique de l’Ouest. Cette circulation donne au film une dimension régionale, tout en maintenant un ancrage fort dans l’histoire mandingue. Présenté en première mondiale à Visions du Réel 2026, en Suisse, « Djeliya, mémoire du Mandé » y a obtenu une mention spéciale du jury. Sa sélection à Lausanne prolonge ce parcours international et offre une nouvelle visibilité à un patrimoine où se croisent histoire, oralité, musique et transmission entre générations. Une reconnaissance qui renforce également la portée du documentaire. Joseph Amara Dembélé

items.title: Roger Federer se cae del olimpo de los milmillonarios en una mañana y solo un año después de alcanzarlo
items.description: No se puede decir que el extenista Roger Federer (Basilea, 45 años) haya empezado bien la semana. El pasado martes, 11 de agosto, el legendario jugador de tenis, retirado de la competición desde septiembre de 2022 , vio cómo su estatus de milmillonario se esfumaba en solo unas horas. Según ha contado la revista económica Forbes , a las 12.30 de aquel mediodía, su patrimonio neto cayó a 952,4 millones de dólares (unos 836 millones de euros al cambio actual), una pérdida de, al menos, 52 millones de dólares. La razón de este repentino varapalo financiero está en el precio de las acciones de la marca suiza de calzado deportivo On Holding, de la que Federer posee acciones, y que a esa misma hora cayó alrededor de un 19%, justo después de anunciar sus decepcionantes resultados en ventas del segundo trimestre del año. items.title: AJK police claim JAAC 'abducted' 8 highway police personnel on election duty
items.description: Azad Jammu Kashmir (AJK) police said on Thursday that eight highway police personnel on election duty had been “abducted” by the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC). Addressing a televised press conference, police spokesperson Khawar Ali Shaukat alleged that the JAAC attacked security forces deputed on election duty in the region. “Eight highway police officials on election duty were abducted,” he said as state media shared a collage of the officials’ pictures. “The personnel are in the custody of JAAC and have been subjected to brutal abuse,” he said. He said that the “miscreants also threatened the families of the personnel that they would be martyred if their demands were not met”. He said that recent events showed that the JAAC was not a peaceful group, but a violent one intent on challenging the state’s writ and weakening institutions. “I want to make it clear that the state was not and is not weak. The state has always shown restraint,” he said, adding that violent acts for the sake of rights were not above the law. He said that the people of the region, by participating in polls in the region, had made it clear that they had nothing to do with the proscribed group. He appealed to the public to disassociate themselves from the JAAC and to not get involved in acts where the state’s writ was challenged. He appealed to parents to keep an eye on their children, saying: ““They play with the future of young people and instigate them against state through misleading propaganda and provocative statements.” At the end of his press conference, he called on the JAAC to free the abducted personnel. “The state will not accept any pressure with regards to the lives of these officials. If the personnel are harmed, obstacles are created in their release or threats to their families continue, the state will not show any leniency,” he said. “If the state’s writ is challenged and if state officials are subjected to violence … the state will carry out its duties in accordance with the law and the Constitution,” he said, vowing strict action against such elements. “Any group that challenges the state’s writ will be dealt with accordingly,” he said. The JAAC, which has been demanding the abolishment of 12 seats in the local legislature reserved for refugees from Indian-held Kashmir, has been holding protests in the region for several weeks now. Clashes took place between protesters and law enforcement personnel in Rawalakot and Mirpur on July 28, which reportedly resulted in several casualties. Amid the tensions, elections are being held across the region in phases. The government has accused militant elements “pursuing a foreign agenda and backed by Indian funding” of fomenting the unrest. Last week, AJK Information Secretary Muhammad Rashid Hanif said that seven law enforcement personnel, including those from police and Rangers, were martyred during recent unrest in the region.

items.title: Mondial féminin FIBA 2026 : Les Aigles Dames accélèrent leur préparation
items.description: © Daou À moins d’un mois de la Coupe du monde féminine de la FIBA, prévue du 4 au 13 septembre à Berlin, la sélection malienne intensifie sa préparation. Après le regroupement de Bamako, un stage en Espagne et plusieurs matches amicaux doivent permettre au groupe d’Oumarou Sidiya d’affûter ses armes. Les Aigles Dames sont regroupées à Bamako depuis le 23 juillet 2026, pour la première étape d’une préparation articulée autour de trois phases. Plusieurs cadres ont déjà rejoint le groupe, tandis que d’autres sont encore attendues. Sous la direction du sélectionneur Oumarou Sidiya, le staff technique s’emploie à placer l’équipe dans les meilleures conditions avant le rendez-vous mondial. Ce regroupement doit se poursuivre jusqu’au 23 août prochain. La sélection malienne devrait ensuite s’envoler pour l’Espagne, où elle participera à un tournoi triangulaire face à l’Espagne et à la Chine avant de disputer un match amical contre le Nigeria. Elle ralliera ensuite Berlin pour achever sa préparation sur place. Deux joueuses majeures, Sika Koné et Aïcha Coulibaly, actuellement engagées en WNBA, aux États-Unis, sont notamment attendues. La sélection enregistre également le retour de Mariam Coulibaly. Longtemps absente de l’équipe nationale, l’intérieure malienne a repris les entraînements avec ses coéquipières et devrait participer à la compétition. Franchir la phase de groupes Logé dans le groupe A avec le Japon, l’Espagne et l’Allemagne, pays-hôte, le Mali devra rapidement trouver son rythme. Pour Amadou Kouyaté, journaliste sportif, la mission s’annonce particulièrement exigeante. « Les rencontres ne seront pas faciles. Toutes les équipes qualifiées viendront avec l’ambition d’aller le plus loin possible et d’atteindre le dernier carré », prévient-il. Selon lui, les Aigles Dames doivent se fixer comme premier objectif de franchir la phase de groupes et de se mêler à la course aux quarts de finale. Au sein de la sélection, la confiance est de mise. « Nous avons déjà passé deux semaines ensemble. Les préparatifs vont bon train et l’ambiance est bonne dans le groupe », assure Oumarou Sidiya. Le technicien malien veut surtout tirer les enseignements de la précédente participation. « L’équipe ambitionne de faire mieux que lors de la dernière édition : gagner des matches en poule et atteindre les quarts de finale. Pour y parvenir, nous devons mieux négocier nos entames de match et éviter de laisser trop d’espaces. Nous savons que notre groupe est difficile, mais c’est le niveau d’une Coupe du monde », souligne-t-il. Le Mali débutera la compétition contre le Japon le 4 septembre, avant d’affronter l’Espagne le lendemain, puis l’Allemagne le 7 septembre. Ali Sankaré

items.title: Dialogue interreligieux : « Les appels à la paix ne suffisent pas, il faut le montrer par l’exemple », dixit Dr Koudbi Kaboré, historien
items.description: L'Association Jeunes Faiseurs de Paix a posé ses valises le mercredi 12 août 2026 dans l'Arrondissement 11 de Ouagadougou pour la huitième étape de sa Caravane « Graines de Cohésion ». Lancée en novembre 2025, cette initiative entend faire du dialogue interreligieux et intercommunautaire un rempart contre les divisions, dans un contexte national marqué par des défis sécuritaires et sociaux. En marge de la cérémonie, Dr Koudbi Kaboré, maître de conférences en histoire à l’Université Joseph Ki‑Zerbo, a souligné dans sa communication que le dialogue doit devenir un vécu, pas un simple discours. La huitième étape de la Caravane « Graines de Cohésion » ne s'est pas limitée à une simple visite protocolaire dans l'Arrondissement 11 de Ouagadougou. Elle a été marquée par des échanges profonds autour du dialogue interreligieux, animés par des figures religieuses et académiques. L'enseignant-chercheur invitant les participants à dépasser la simple tolérance L'enseignant-chercheur Koudbi Kaboré, maître de conférences en histoire à l’Université Joseph Ki‑Zerbo, intervenant sur le thème du dialogue interreligieux comme outil de consolidation de la paix, a partagé l'expérience des communautés chrétiennes et musulmanes de Dori, qui vivent en harmonie depuis les années 1970. L'enseignant-chercheur a invité les participants à dépasser la simple tolérance. « La tolérance ne suffit pas. Quand vous allez au-delà de la tolérance, le dialogue veut dire que vous pouvez être ensemble, travailler ensemble pour relever les défis communs », a-t-il expliqué, appelant à faire du dialogue un vécu quotidien plutôt qu'un simple discours. « Les appels à la paix ne suffisent pas, il faut le montrer par l'exemple », a précisé l'enseignant-chercheur. Pour Dr Kaboré, « en situation de méfiance, on a besoin de discours rassurants, de gens qui émergent pour donner de l'espoir ». Il estime par ailleurs que « la force contre les crises, c'est de ne pas se laisser diviser davantage ». L'historien a également souligné que la crise, bien qu'éprouvante, doit servir à consolider les liens entre les communautés. Dr Kaboré a en conséquence appelé à dépasser les préjugés et à s'unir pour travailler ensemble, allant ainsi au-delà des différences. L'imam Alidou Ilboudo rappelant le rôle fondamental des guides spirituels dans l'édification de la nation Le président du Centre culturel islamique du Burkina (CCIB), Imam Alidou Ilboudo, a renchéri en rappelant le rôle fondamental des guides spirituels dans l'édification de la nation. « Le leader religieux, dans le contexte actuel de notre pays, doit contribuer à construire la nation par des paroles fortes et par l'engagement personnel, ainsi que celui de ses disciples, et non pas être celui qui va contribuer à la destruction ou être à la source de divisions », a-t-il martelé. L'imam Ilboudo a mis en garde contre toute instrumentalisation de la foi à des fins de division, insistant sur l'idée que la religion doit relier les hommes à Dieu et, par là même, les rendre utiles à l'humanité tout entière. « En islam, on dit que l'humanité est la famille de Dieu, et celui que Dieu aime le plus est celui qui est utile à la famille de Dieu », a-t-il souligné. L'assistance était composé des différentes couches de la société Les échanges entre les communicateurs et les participants, parmi lesquels des chefs coutumiers et des leaders religieux, ont permis de rappeler que la paix se construit au quotidien, dans les familles, les lieux de culte et les quartiers, loin des seules grandes décisions institutionnelles. Lire aussi : Burkina | Caravane de la Paix « Graines de Cohésion » : Le dialogue devient le terreau de la résilience Mathias KAM Minute.bf

items.title: Désinformation : La jeunesse à l’avant-garde de la lutte
items.description: © Daou Placée au cœur du thème de la Semaine nationale de la jeunesse 2026, la lutte contre la désinformation s’impose comme un volet à part entière des enjeux de paix et de sécurité. Les formations au fact-checking, la sensibilisation des blogueurs et la mobilisation des influenceurs se multiplient afin de mieux armer les jeunes face aux contenus trompeurs et aux discours de haine. Sur les réseaux sociaux, une image sortie de son contexte, une vidéo ancienne présentée comme récente ou une rumeur relayée en chaîne peuvent rapidement toucher des milliers d’utilisateurs. Dans un environnement marqué par les tensions sécuritaires et communautaires, la circulation de contenus trompeurs a progressivement fait de l’espace numérique un autre terrain des enjeux de paix et de cohésion sociale. Lors d’une conférence régionale organisée à Bamako en juillet 2025, plusieurs acteurs avaient souligné que les fausses informations pouvaient alimenter les tensions intercommunautaires, éroder la confiance envers les institutions et favoriser l’exposition aux discours extrémistes. Les jeunes figurent parmi les publics particulièrement ciblés par certaines campagnes de désinformation. Apprendre à vérifier Face à la multiplication des contenus, l’un des principaux enjeux réside dans l’éducation aux médias et à l’information. En novembre 2025, la 3 ème Académie des jeunes blogueurs du Mali a été consacrée au rôle des influenceurs numériques dans la lutte contre la désinformation. Avec l’appui de l’UNESCO, les participants ont été initiés au fact-checking, au journalisme sensible aux conflits et aux outils permettant d’évaluer la fiabilité d’une information. Dans la même dynamique, l’Association des blogueurs du Mali a formé, à la fin de 2025, 120 jeunes à Bamako, Sikasso et Gao sur la gestion de la désinformation, la vérification des faits et la citoyenneté numérique. Le défi dépasse toutefois le cadre des formations ponctuelles. Faire de la jeunesse un rempart durable suppose de diffuser plus largement les réflexes de vérification, notamment en apprenant à identifier les sources, à confronter les versions, à vérifier les images et à éviter le partage immédiat. Dans la lutte contre la désinformation, le renforcement de l’esprit critique apparaît comme l’un des principaux moyens de faire face à la rapidité de diffusion des contenus trompeurs. Mohamed Kenouvi

items.title: François Hollande prépare une rentrée en «quasi-candidat» pour 2027
items.description: Voir cette publication sur Instagram Une publication partagée par François Hollande (@fhollande) Francois Hollande, en villegiature en Correze, a passe un ete studieux. a la veille de son anniversaire, le 12 août, il finalisait les dernieres corrections de son ouvrage Unir, nouveau monde, nouvelle gauche , qui sortira le 3 septembre aux editions Robert Laffont. Ce texte doit lui permettre d'exposer sa vision et une dizaine de propositions pour « prouver qu'il a change ». Livre, debat et universites d'ete au programme La rentree s'annonce dense. Fin août, l'ancien chef de l'etat participera aux universites d'ete du Parti socialiste a Blois, une premiere depuis longtemps. Le meme week-end, il debattra face a edouard Philippe, favori du bloc central. Une confrontation qu'il appelle de ses vœux et qui sera scrutee de pres. Ses proches ont marque le coup pour ses 72 ans en placardant quelque 500 affiches « Lui president… » a travers la France (et jusqu'au Japon), vantant des elements de son bilan : reduction du deficit, retraites a 60 ans pour 650 000 Francais, mariage pour les personnes de meme sexe… Cette petite campagne d'affichage a suscite de nombreuses moqueries sur les reseaux sociaux pour un president qui avait fini son quinquennat avec une cote de popularite historiquement basse. Totalement irresponsable. Qui paye? https://t.co/tDVPW0EuHv pic.twitter.com/ZjgCuOqM17 — Sylvain Catherine (@sc_cath) August 12, 2026 « Ce n'est pas un lancement de campagne », assurent-ils, tout en entretenant l'hypothese d'un retour. Hollande et Bernard Cazeneuve ont choisi de ne pas s'inscrire a la primaire socialiste d'octobre, laissant le champ libre a Raphael Glucksmann. « On est en deuxieme rideau. [...] S'il arrete de pedaler, nous sommes la », confie un proche. Francois Hollande entend se montrer rassurant et consensuel, mais il est conspue par une partie de la gauche melenchoniste et socialiste. La photo publiee sur ses reseaux sociaux le montrant en relecture a ete tres discutee. Le journaliste Alexis Poulain a ainsi commente l'image en evoquant le coût de ses chaises de jardin : 600 euros piece, rappelant que l'ancien chef de l'etat emargeait a 35 000 euros par mois. François Hollande, sur une chaise de jardin à 600€, incarne-t-il parfaitement le Parti Socialiste ? 🤔💰 pic.twitter.com/xWpKI3lCMw — Alexis Poulin (@Poulin2012) August 12, 2026 L'ancien president mise sur une montee en puissance dans les sondages de stature presidentielle et sur un eventuel vote utile contre les « extremes ». Il a multiplie les rendez-vous avec de grands mecenes (Leclerc, Medef, Axa, TotalEnergies…) et reuni soutiens et relais d'opinion.
